sa.translation_status_note: No single classical everyday utensil term; this is a descriptive noun for a pronged implement.

grc.translation_status_note: Classical Greek lacks a standard everyday utensil term for a dining fork; this is an approximate ‘prong/pin’ term.

non.translation_status_note: A dining fork is not native to Old Norse usage; this is the usual later loanword.

grc.translation_status_note: A later diminutive utensil term; classical Greek more often uses broader words like κοχλιάς for spoon-like implement.

ar-classical.translation_status_note: A post-classical/learned noun for a spoon; pre-1200 Classical Arabic lacks a fully native everyday term for the modern utensil sense.

la.translation_status_note: Classical Latin has no exact everyday native term for a round deep dish; "poculum" is only approximate and can mean cup/drinking vessel.

sa.translation_status_note: Modern loanword for a cup in the drinking-vessel sense.

ar-classical.translation_status_note: Later cup/drinking-vessel term; not securely pre-1200 classical.

sa.translation_status_note: Modern loanword used for a dining plate.

non.translation_status_note: Native Old Norse usually has simpler dish/bowl terms; this form is a learned borrowing used for a plate-like dish.
